articles.title_zh: Army sergeant pleads guilty to selling military secrets to China
articles.content_orig:
The front gate at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash. (Stars and Stripes)
By JENNIFER H. SVAN STARS AND STRIPES
A U.S. Army sergeant faces up to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty Monday to conspiring to sell U.S. military secrets to China.
Jian Zhao, 37, was serving on active duty at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state when he used his access and position to gather national defense information and equipment that he sold and transferred to individuals in China, according to the U.S. Justice Department.
Among the documents federal prosecutors say Zhao handed over were excerpts from technical manuals for operating the HIMARS multiple-rocket launcher, a weapons system that Ukraine has deployed in its war with Russia. The Justice Department also said Zhao provided sensitive information related to U.S. military readiness in the event of an armed conflict with China and offered military computers and government hard drives for sale.
Prosecutors described the military materials he sold as sensitive, secret or top secret. He photographed controlled military documents using his personal cellphone and removed government property and military storage devices without authorization, they said.
According to the U.S. Department of Justice, this surveillance footage shows Jian Zhao, an active-duty U.S. Army sergeant stationed at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, photographing restricted military documents and presentations at his desk. (U.S. Department of Justice)
A battery supply sergeant, Zhao enlisted in 2017. The conspiracy occurred from November 2021 through March 2025, according to federal prosecutors. Zhao received payments totaling $15,000 in exchange for gathering the electronic media, documents and other military information and sharing it with conspirators in China, prosecutors said.
Zhao entered his plea Monday in federal court in Portland with the help of a Mandarin interpreter, The Oregonian reported.
U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford speaks during a Department of Justice event.  Bradford announced charges against Army Sgt. Jian Zhao, who pleaded guilty to selling classified military information to China. (Facebook)
“Members of the United States military are entrusted with protecting some of our nation’s most sensitive information and capabilities,” said Scott Bradford, U.S. attorney for the District of Oregon, in a statement Monday.
Zhao “violated that trust by exploiting his access to military information and equipment for personal profit while knowingly providing materials to individuals linked to China,” Bradford said.
Zhao was assigned to the 17 th Field Artillery Brigade when federal agents arrested him March 6, 2025, at his residence in Lacey, Washington, where they recovered approximately $30,000 in cash, electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives.
Zhao is the second of three co-defendants to plead guilty in federal court in Portland, Oregon, in connection with the scheme.
Former soldier Ruoyu Duan, 41, pleaded guilty in September to a single count of conspiracy to gather and transmit national defense information, according to the Justice Department. He admitted to connecting Zhao and Capt. Li Tian to Chinese buyers and facilitating transactions between them. He is scheduled to be sentence Dec. 10.
Zhao is scheduled to be sentenced March 1.
Under the terms of the plea agreement, Zhao agreed to forfeit $17,500 as proceeds of the offense and abandon his interest in approximately $30,000 seized during the investigation.
He faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a fine of $250,000. Prosecutors, however, indicated they plan to seek the low end of a sentencing guideline calculation for Zhao that will be based on his conduct and criminal history, The Oregonian reported Monday. As part of his plea agreement, Zhao will not challenge a dishonorable discharge from the military and accepted a lifetime obligation to protect classified and defense information, according to The Oregonian.
Jennifer H. Svan reports on the U.S. military from Kaiserslautern, Germany, where she writes about the Air Force, Army and DODEA schools. She’s had previous assignments for Stars and Stripes in Japan, reporting from Yokota and Misawa air bases. Before Stripes, she worked for daily newspapers in Wyoming and Colorado. She’s a graduate of the College of William and Mary in Virginia.

articles.title_zh: Stock futures decline as Nvidia pulls back, giving back part of Monday’s rally: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday.
"It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now."
Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure.
"Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary."
Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership.
"If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said.
Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates.
Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet.
"There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said.
"These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target."

articles.title_orig: Cardinal Fernández: ‘The Diary reveals Francis’ heart and his spirituality’
articles.title_zh: Cardinal Fernández: ‘The Diary reveals Francis’ heart and his spirituality’
articles.content_orig:
Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.
In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.
In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.
Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign .
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.
"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.
He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.
"I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".
The collection of diaries was edited by a longtime friend of Francis
The late pope also revealed that while getting ready to go to sleep in June 2018, he "saw the gates of hell".
"I watched a little, and it terrified me," he said, adding that he "took the rosary as a weapon".
"It's dangerous to get close to the gates of hell, because flames can spring out and burn," he wrote.
Cardinal Victor Fernandez, head of the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and friend of Francis, edited the diaries, which are the first by a pope to be released to the public since the 1960s.
Pope Francis was elected pope in 2013 and died aged 88 in April 2025.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi PM orders ministry to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish control, Kurds reject move
articles.title_zh: Iraqi PM orders ministry to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish control, Kurds reject move
articles.content_orig:
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous region in the north of the country.
The prime minister’s order covers oilfields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces, according to a statement from his office on Tuesday.
It said Baghdad would “secure and monitor all oilfields with cameras, including fields within the administrative boundaries of the federal government that are under the security authority of the regional government”.
Al-Zaidi also ordered the border crossings authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdish region and directed the regional government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal Oil Ministry.
“The Border Forces Command shall close unofficial crossings along the international borders with neighbouring countries, including crossings in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq,” the statement said, adding that “all seasonal roads” between the four governorates and the Kurdish region would be closed.
Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Baghdad, said the latest development might exacerbate tensions and disputes over control of oil and the sharing of budgetary resources between the national government and the autonomous regional government.
“The federal government is keen to keep all excavation and marketing of oil under its state organisation, SOMO, but this has been totally rejected by the Kurdish region,” he said.
A dispute over Kurdish authorities selling oil without Baghdad’s approval halted pipeline shipments to Turkiye for more than two years before the sides agreed in September 2025 to restart them.
Al-Zaidi, meanwhile, removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company’s director general and his deputies pending further investigation, Iraq’s state news agency reported.
In a separate case, Iraqi officials accused Kataib Hezbollah, an armed group backed by Iran, of running an oil smuggling network in its stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad.
The group denied the accusation.

articles.title_orig: China walks ‘thin line’ in push to prevent another Horn of Africa war
articles.title_zh: China walks ‘thin line’ in push to prevent another Horn of Africa war
articles.content_orig:
Beijing, China – China has stepped up diplomatic efforts in the Horn of Africa, sending senior envoys to four countries to ease mounting tensions that threaten to plunge the region into another devastating conflict.
Beijing’s special representative for African affairs, Liu Xianfa, travelled to Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early November, while its special envoy for Horn of Africa affairs, Hu Changchun, visited Eritrea. They met senior officials, including Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and the foreign ministers of Ethiopia and Egypt.
Announcing the visits on November 2, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said they were aimed at “promoting talks for peace, easing tensions, and playing a constructive role for upholding regional peace and stability”.
The visits followed a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, raising fears of another war between the neighbours. Meanwhile, longstanding disputes involving Egypt threaten to draw other countries into a wider confrontation.
Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a devastating border war between 1998 and 2000, killing tens of thousands of people. A historic peace agreement in 2018 ended two decades of hostility, but their reconciliation began to unravel following Ethiopia’s civil war in the northern Tigray region.
Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian government troops against Tigrayan fighters, but Eritrea was excluded from the 2022 peace agreement that ended the main phase of the war.
Central to their latest dispute is Ethiopia’s push to secure access to the Red Sea. The country has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993 and relies heavily on neighbouring Djibouti’s ports for international trade. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed argues access to the sea is essential for his country’s future, but his government’s interest in Eritrea’s strategic port of Assab has raised fears in Asmara over its territorial sovereignty.
Both governments accuse each other of supporting armed groups.
Complicating matters is Ethiopia’s longstanding dispute with Egypt over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile. Cairo fears the project could threaten its water supply, while Addis Ababa insists it has the right to harness the river for electricity generation and economic development.
Egypt has strengthened its relationship with Eritrea, adding another dimension to the growing tensions. Recent reports of Ethiopian and Eritrean troops gathering near their shared border have heightened fears of a wider conflict.
China has billions of dollars at stake in the Horn of Africa, which sits along one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes. Between 2000 and 2023, China committed $17.8bn in loans to Ethiopia, according to United States-based research institute AidData.
Edson Ziso, a visiting research fellow at the University of Adelaide, says China has played a “starring role” in Ethiopia’s economic transformation. Among Beijing’s flagship infrastructure projects is the $4.3bn Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, which connects landlocked Ethiopia to the coast.
Meanwhile, Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military base, which opened in 2017. The country sits near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a crucial shipping passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. “The Strait of Hormuz stalemate has already highlighted the huge cost conflict can inflict on the global economy when vital shipping lanes are choked,” says Ziso.
China’s efforts also reflect President Xi Jinping’s desire to portray his country as a major diplomatic player and contributor to global peace and stability, say analysts. Beijing has promoted what it calls the “Outlook on Peace and Development in the Horn of Africa”, a 2022 framework that emphasises African-led solutions to security challenges.
Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow with the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, says Beijing’s approach is focused on helping countries in the region “control their security destiny”, rather than imposing solutions from outside. She says Beijing’s view is that “development gaps fuel instability,” but success depends on all parties accepting that “confrontation leaves all of them worse off.”
China’s close relationships with governments across the region put it in a position to encourage dialogue, but its ability to broker meaningful compromises remains unclear.
Beijing’s principle of noninterference has helped it cultivate relationships across Africa. Yet the disputes involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt concern deeply sensitive questions of territory, sovereignty and water security. Economic incentives may not be enough to resolve them, caution analysts.
Among the obstacles, Khan says, are actors outside the region who have “stoked confrontation and disrupted African-led processes”. Ziso says the involvement of proxy forces, fighter groups and rebels also presents a significant challenge.
And while all regional countries have close ties with Beijing, some, particularly Egypt, have longstanding security relationships with Washington. Ziso says this could limit China’s ability to achieve a breakthrough if governments perceive Chinese-led solutions as jeopardising relations with the US.
Against that backdrop, China’s recent diplomatic visits have produced statements of support for greater cooperation and regional peace, but no formal negotiations or concrete agreements have been announced.
“China is thus walking a thin line,” Ziso says, adding that all four countries – Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti – are critical to Beijing’s economic and strategic interests. “China may need to look beyond its own interests in pursuit of concrete and sustainable de-escalation.”

articles.title_orig: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.title_zh: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.content_orig:
China has sentenced a government official to death for handing over state secrets and classified documents to a foreign intelligence agent.
In a public post, Monday, China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection said the convicted official was approached and recruited by a foreign woman while working overseas.
It is extremely rare for China to disclose that it has sentenced someone to death for espionage, or publish details on proceedings involving national security.
The post did not mention where the official was posted, but gave his surname as Ma, and said he had been approached by a woman named ‘Kailin,’ who initially said she was interested to learn Chinese. It did not say what the woman’s nationality was.
After their relationship developed, ‘Kailin’ began shifting their chats to “politically sensitive” topics and major international developments, and convinced Ma to hand over sensitive information about the personnel and operations of a Chinese institution in the country, according to prosecutors.
Kailin later introduced Ma to her other colleagues and told him that if he did not become an agent for their country, they would tip off the Chinese government about his activities. Ma then signed a pledge of loyalty, starting down the path “being consumed by darkness, and doomed beyond redemption,” the statement said.
The official later returned to China and sent “hundreds” of classified intelligence documents to the foreign agent in return for a fixed monthly income with additional bonus when he provided key material, according to the statement.
China’s prosecutor found Ma sent nine documents classified as state secrets and 26 documents classified as confidential in return for more than $150,000 for the espionage activities.
The state secrets administration’s post offered a stern warning to Chinese citizens to “maintain vigilance in our social and personal lives, adhere strictly to workplace discipline, and guard against being targeted, manipulated or exploited by hostile actors.”
The verdict comes as China steps up its anti-espionage efforts as its strategic rivalry with the US-led west deepens.
In 2023 China broadened the scope of its already sweeping counter-espionage law to expand the definition of espionage from covering state secrets and intelligence to any “documents, data, materials or items related to national security and interests,” without specifying specific parameters for how these terms are defined.
Earlier this year its spy agency warned that China’s young people were being duped by foreign forces into shirking hard work and prioritizing their individual emotions at the expense of national development.
The post from the State Security Ministry’s official account warned young people to stay vigilant against “complex opinion traps” and any “lying flat” narratives that propagate the message that hard work is futile.

articles.title_zh: For China, Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia Is a Mixed Blessing
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Eleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds.
On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)
But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”
The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession.
But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return.
Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.
The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.
But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.
And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.
Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.
The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis.
It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.
But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.
The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology.
But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.
With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.
The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times , alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse.
Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee.
But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks."
As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.
That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions.
“Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday.
Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.
Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic stock falls as Monday's tech rally takes off
articles.title_zh: Anthropic stock falls as Monday's tech rally takes off
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Just two days after its public debut, the stock market's newest AI giant, Anthropic ( ANT ), looks to be missing out on Monday's major tech rally.
Anthropic's stock briefly fell below its $83 IPO price during premarket trading on Tuesday, extending its slide. The stock fell 5% to $82.95 at 06:43 ET.
The stock of the Claude model maker fell 1.4% on Monday, trading below $88 as of 3:00 p.m. ET after whipsawing earlier in the day. Meanwhile, Nvidia ( NVDA ) and other AI-linked stocks, including CoreWeave ( CRWV ), soared amid the broader tech rebound that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
The move comes after Anthropic's stock sank 9% on Friday following a 17% gain on its IPO day last Thursday. At Monday's current price, the stock is up about 5% from its $83 IPO price.
Read more: What investors should know about buying into Anthropic stock
The choppy performance might reflect ordinary post IPO profit-taking and broader skepticism about Anthropic's valuation. Needham analysts said in a Sunday note that the most common concern they hear from investors is whether the company can sustain its enormous revenue growth next year. The company's fully diluted IPO valuation of about $1.5 trillion is roughly 40 times trailing sales.
The stock also has a potential supply overhang. As much as 315 million shares held by insiders, roughly one-third of the stock the company issued in its IPO, became eligible for sale almost immediately, according to Anthropic's IPO paperwork.
Needham added that given Anthropic's staggered schedule for permitting insider share sales could bring more shares to market in the first six months.
Another key question hanging over the company is how credit markets will absorb the AI firm's massive spending needs. Anthropic has committed to spending about $900 billion on its computing and infrastructure needs for the next two decades , including $70 billion due over the next 12 months.
The AI boom's ravenous capital needs have flooded the bond market this year, becoming a looming concern for investors.
Investors expect the major rating agencies to assign a high-yield, or junk, rating to the company's debt, according to a Wall Street Journal report . No rating has yet been announced.
Anthropic's credit rating is key for the wider AI ecosystem. Getting the higher investment-grade rating would help offer some relief to chip makers, including Nvidia and Broadcom ( AVGO ), that have guaranteed billions of dollars worth of microchips to customers that lease compute power to major model makers like Anthropic and rival OpenAI. ( OPAI.PVT )
The high-yield bond market also comes with constraints, including smaller capacity and higher borrowing rates, for the newly public giant.

articles.title_orig: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
articles.title_zh: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
articles.content_orig:
Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli has condemned Ukraine’s deadly attack on a Russian warship in Libya, in what Kyiv claimed was an “exemplary” operation.
Libya’s Foreign Ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine war and that its sovereignty and territorial integrity were non-negotiable, according to a statement posted on Facebook on Monday.
“The continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct military operations on Libyan territory or in its territorial waters,” it said.
Sunday’s drone strike on the Merkury, one of Moscow’s newest warships, resulted in the deaths of at least 10 Libyan and Russian crew members, local authorities said.
The attack sent shockwaves through Europe and the Middle East and raised new fears that the months-long war had already spilled over far from the front line.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Ukraine’s attacks represented a “very dangerous trend”.
On Sunday, Ukrainian drones targeted the Merkury in Libya’s coastal city of Benghazi after the Russian corvette docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s eastern rival government based in Benghazi. It is led by Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA), which is based in Tobruk.
Sources told Al Jazeera that the warship was moored in the civilian area of Benghazi seaport, close to a naval base, when it was hit.
In a Monday post on X, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that the attack had been carried out by Ukraine’s intelligence security service, the SBU, and involved seven Ukrainian drones. The strike also destroyed a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter. A second Russian ship was also hit. Zelenskyy said the cargo vessel Angara was transporting weapons.
“Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” he wrote.
Ukraine’s security service justified the attacks in a Monday statement, saying that both vessels were “legitimate military targets for Ukraine because they directly supported Russia’s military capabilities”.
Satellite images on Sunday showed that most of the vessel ‌‌‌‌had capsized, with only its bow still visible above water. Smoke from the initial explosion rose from the ship’s superstructure. Along the pier, debris from the strike lay scattered around.
However, officials in Libya told the Associated Press that the Merkury was only heavily damaged.
Unnamed sources also told AP that Ukraine had launched the drones from a military base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.
Tripoli, in its condemnation of the attack on Monday, did not confirm Ukraine’s alleged presence.
Earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Osama Hammad of the eastern Libyan government said it had submitted an investigation request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.
Oil-rich Libya is a focal point of the long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The North African country has been divided since 2011, when a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. Moscow’s close ally was killed later that year.
The UN recognises the western Libyan government in Tripoli, while the Benghazi-based administration in the east is a close ally of Moscow. Russia has long maintained deep ties with Haftar in a bid to keep eastern Libya as a logistical hub for its widening military operations across Africa, including in Sudan and the Sahel region.
In 2024, following the fall of the Russia-aligned regime of Bashar al-Assad, Moscow shifted attention to Libya as a potential new site for the vast military infrastructure it had built up in Syria over the previous decade during the civil war there.
Moscow managed to maintain relations with the new government in Damascus, although its footprint is much smaller, according to analysis by the Atlantic Council think tank. Some estimates put the number of Russian troops there at 1,000, significantly fewer than around 10,000 in previous years.
Russia is believed to have planned and funded projects at multiple Haftar-controlled Libyan military bases in its search for a “plan B” following the fall of the Assad regime in Syria: Al-Jufra, Al-Khadim, Al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati, Maaten al-Sarra and Tamanhint.
An estimated 1,800 Russian troops, including those from Africa Corps, which succeeded the paramilitary Wagner Group, are presently based in Libya.
The United States is meanwhile leading efforts to reunite the two Libyan militaries, partly to counter Russia, analysts say, with Washington focusing on relations with the 35-year-old LNA deputy commander and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar.
That is likely why Moscow has not yet secured a port in the southern Mediterranean: Libya’s eastern authorities do not want to damage improving ties with the US, Turkiye and European partners by giving Moscow port access, which would be more visible and invite scrutiny, unlike the inland military bases, the Atlantic Council noted.
It means that Ukraine is achieving results in its push to target Russia thousands of kilometres from the battlefield with what Zelenskyy calls “long-range sanctions”, even as Moscow has focused on overwhelming Kyiv with swarms of killer drones daily.
A particular focus is Russia’s so-called ‘shadow fleet’ , the network of tankers Moscow uses to evade Western oil sanctions.
Around the same time the Merkury was hit, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound dry cargo ship Sparta II in the eastern Baltic Sea, near Finland. Finnish authorities blamed Kyiv, while Moscow called it “terrorism”.
In July, Kyiv said it hit a Russian missile boat and the Iran-linked cargo ship, Anna, in the Caspian Sea, resulting in a diplomatic fallout between Tehran and Kyiv.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have also hit deep inside Russia, targeting oil terminals and other energy infrastructure.
In June 2025, Ukraine’s secret service smuggled components of 117 attack drones into Russia, then arranged and deployed them to hit multiple military bases in five regions. The covert operation, nicknamed Operation Spider’s Web, caused around $7bn in damage to Russian military equipment.
In the Sahel region of western Africa, Ukraine has been accused of working with armed groups fighting against Malian forces and their allied Africa Corps members, although Kyiv denies that.

articles.title_orig: Sanofi strikes $41bn deal as patent cliff looms
articles.title_zh: Sanofi strikes $41bn deal as patent cliff looms
articles.content_orig:
Insmed shares rallied 14% in premarket trading Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.
The acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.
It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff , when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire.
If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.
Insmed shares rose 14.6% to $170.86 in early premarket trading, while Sanofi stock rose 6% in Paris.
Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside.
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.
Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop towards the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.
Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026 , as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets, and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026.
While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity.
"Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.
Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA , Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate , following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.
The Insmed deal is a good strategic fit that will help soften the blow from Dupixent's expected 2031–32 loss of exclusivity, said Jefferies analysts.
Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases.
"The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition.
"Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement.
Sanofi shares fell 2.9%, and Insmed rose 24% on Nov. 19 after Bloomberg reported that a deal was underway.

articles.title_orig: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.title_zh: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.content_orig:
Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.
But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule . She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.
India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ârequest for comment. In April, âthe ministry said it was â examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.
What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.
The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.
Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.
The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.
"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.
India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration .
The court on Monday upheld Denmark 's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration . The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU . Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.

Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

articles.title_orig: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.title_zh: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.content_orig:
China's automotive transformation is creating a new set of industrial capabilities that could benefit the global automotive industry as a whole.
Over the past decade, China has developed a highly interconnected automotive ecosystem, bringing together battery technology, intelligent driving, vehicle software, advanced manufacturing, and an increasingly sophisticated supply chain.
The significance of this transformation lies not only in the competitiveness of Chinese automakers, but also in the opportunities these capabilities create for companies around the world.
Volkswagen offers an interesting example. The group is targeting annual exports of around 300,000 vehicles from China by 2030. More importantly, it plans to introduce China-developed vehicle platforms and electronic architecture into selected overseas markets，which represents a meaningful evolution in the role of China within multinational automakers' global operations.
Image source: Volkswagen Group China
For decades, international automotive companies brought technology, manufacturing expertise, management practices, and engineering capabilities to China. These contributions played an important role in the development of China's automotive industry.
Today, we are beginning to see industrial capabilities flow in the other direction as well.
Chinese companies are expanding their manufacturing, engineering, and supply-chain operations overseas. Meanwhile, multinational companies are increasingly integrating China's innovation resources into their global development strategies.
This is not simply a reversal of traditional globalization. It is an evolution toward a more interconnected model of industrial collaboration.
Different markets still have their own strengths. China's rapidly evolving technology ecosystem can complement Europe's engineering expertise, Japan's manufacturing and quality management capabilities, and the growing industrial capacity of emerging markets.
The opportunity is not to replicate the Chinese automotive model everywhere, but to combine complementary capabilities and develop solutions that meet different local needs.
Of course, this transformation brings challenges. Companies must navigate regulatory differences, cultural expectations, financial pressures, and increasingly complex localization requirements.
These challenges also highlight the importance of deeper industrial collaboration, local capability building, and disciplined long-term investment.
For global automotive executives, the strategic question should therefore extend beyond how to compete with Chinese companies. It should also be about how to leverage China's industrial capabilities, integrate them with existing strengths, and create better products and sustainable businesses for consumers around the world .
In my view, the greatest value of China's automotive transformation will not be measured solely by the number of vehicles Chinese companies sell globally. It will also be measured by how much this transformation contributes to the evolution of the entire global automotive industry.
That is a much greater opportunity than winning a car war.

articles.title_orig: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.title_zh: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.title_zh: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.
"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.
The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.
The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.
Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.
The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.
To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.
"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said . "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."
Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon , an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.
Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.
"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.
OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.
"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."
"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative ."

articles.title_zh: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.content_orig:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests , said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Imposes Sanctions on Megaspeed, Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Imposes Sanctions on Megaspeed, Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors.
The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a filing from Commerceâs Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata. âThese additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,â the filing reads. âThese entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.â
Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.
âThe Commerce Department placed Megaspeed on the Entity List. This makes it unlawful to export any US-origin goods, software, or technology to Megaspeed,â BIS spokesman Thomas Wackman told Semafor. âIt is also now unlawful to export advanced SI chips to Megaspeed, even if the chips are produced outside the United States. Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings.â
